1:
Before the salutation is glossed, several commentators stop to ask why there is a second letter at all. Chrysostom answers it twice over. Paul had promised in the first epistle to come, and promised it again more mildly toward the end; yet after a long interval he still had not come, the Spirit detaining him in matters of far greater necessity, so that a second letter was needed which would not have been had he only outstayed his time a little. But that is not the whole reason. They were amended by the first: the man they had applauded they cut off, the collection was gathered with much forwardness, and Titus received with fear and trembling. As Paul rebuked them when they were at fault, so on their amendment he should commend them — which is why the letter is not severe throughout but only in a few places toward the end. He adds the complication: there were Jews among them who thought highly of themselves and accused Paul of being a boaster, whose taunt he later quotes back at them, that his letters are weighty but his bodily presence weak and his speech of no account.

Clarke turns the question into a chronology, the most technical thing in the entry. The letter was written about a year after the former, since Achaia is later said to have been ready a year ago; and since Paul meant to stay at Ephesus till Pentecost and is here excusing himself for not wintering in Corinth, it must belong to a new year. He then rehearses Whitby's four arguments that it was written after the second coming into Macedonia: Paul had been at Troas and left it, Timothy was now with him whereas he had gone ahead the first time, Macedonians were likely to accompany him, and the postscript places the writing at Philippi. What prompted it, he adds, was Titus's report in Macedonia: the first epistle had overwhelmed them with distress, led them to examine their state closely, moved them to excommunicate the incestuous man, and filled them with affection for their apostle. Henry gives the same interval and notes that many had shown marks of repentance while others still followed their false teachers — and that because Paul delayed his visit out of unwillingness to treat them severely, they charged him with levity and change of conduct.

On the salutation itself the notes are short and the point is always the false apostles. Gill observes that Paul styles himself an apostle by the will of God where the former letter said called to be one, and thinks the phrase aimed at men who had neither. Calvin states the rule: authority requires a call and fidelity in executing the office, and since the false apostles usurp the title too, the mere name is not enough — he who gives himself out as an apostle must show himself such by his work. He also presses what the address concedes, that a church existed at Corinth amid such a conflux of evils, since the faults of individuals do not prevent a society with genuine marks of religion from being recognised as one. Timothy replaces Sosthenes, and they differ on why. Ellicott takes the brother in its wider sense of fellow-Christian and thinks him Paul's amanuensis; Robertson denies he is co-author in any sense; Barnes gives three motives: he was lately among them, Paul wished to build the authority of a man he expected to succeed him, and his testimony could rebut the charge of insincerity about the changed visit. Wesley notes the usage: writing to Timothy, Paul calls him his son; writing of him, his brother. On Achaia the two agree that the whole Roman province is meant, wide enough to take in Cenchreae. Of the greeting itself none of them has anything to say: five simply refer the reader back.
3:
The letter begins not with thanksgiving but with a benediction, and they all notice the difference. Ellicott calls it something like a doxology, the utterance of a more exulting joy than the simple thanksgivings opening other letters, and finds the same formula in Ephesians. Robertson makes the point from the other side: there is no thanksgiving or prayer here as in the first epistle, because Paul finds his basis for gratitude in God and not in them. Barnes reports from Doddridge that eleven of the thirteen epistles begin with exclamations of praise, and reads this one as prompted by a severe trial lately survived, the passage showing above all that there may be elevated joy in the midst of deep affliction. Calvin gives the opening three purposes at once: to extol the goodness of God, to animate the Corinthians by example to endure persecution, and to magnify himself in pious glorying against the slanders of the false apostles — for such is the world's depravity that it derides martyrdoms it ought to have admired, and seeks reproach in the splendid trophies of the pious.

The three titles are then taken one by one. On the first Henry is the most careful, distinguishing the senses in which God is Father of Christ: of his divine nature by eternal generation, of his human by the conception in the virgin, and of Christ as God-man and Redeemer by covenant-relation, a bond he sets beside the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. On the second, Ellicott weighs whether the genitive is a Hebraism for an adjective, which would make it the merciful Father of Jewish prayers and of the Koran's recurring formula, and prefers the literal sense, that God originates all mercies; Clarke says the same in a line, the source whence all mercy flows, whether of body or soul, time or eternity. On the third Robertson supplies the philology, the noun built on a verb meaning to call to one's side and the very word used of the Spirit as Comforter, while Ellicott adds that it carries counsel as well as consolation and counts it twelve times in this epistle, twenty-eight with the cognate verb. Wesley states the relation between the last two titles: mercies are the fountain of comfort, comfort the outward expression of mercy; God shows mercy in the affliction itself and gives comfort both in it and after it. Calvin adds the condition governing all three, that where Christ is not, the beneficence of God is not.

On why the comfort is given the corpus is unanimous and pointed. Gill says the end was not so much on their own account as for the good of others; Calvin makes it a rule, that God's favours are given not for private advantage but that a man may have more in his power for helping others, the riches of the Spirit being for communicating rather than keeping — chiefly, he adds, by ministers of the Word. Barnes and Robertson make it a principle about experience: only by personal experience can we impart consolation, and affliction in a preacher's life exists to qualify him for ministry, which otherwise turns perfunctory. Clarke puts it as an insult: what a miserable preacher who has all his divinity by study and nothing by experience, for if his heart has not felt the love of God shed abroad in it he can neither instruct the ignorant nor comfort the distressed. Ellicott alone looks outside Scripture, quoting Sophocles that they comfort others who themselves have mourned, and Virgil that not ignorant of ill he too had learnt to succour the suffering — then marking where they stop short, since sorrow alone may lead to sympathy but not to the power of speaking a word in season to the weary. Wesley states the arithmetic: he who has experienced all kinds of affliction can comfort in all.
5:
Whose sufferings are meant is settled the same way by everyone, with differing care. Gill draws the line first: not what Christ endured in his own person in the room and stead of his people, but what he suffers in his members, or they for his sake — abounding in number and weight, yet never more than what Christ bore when he was made sin and a curse. Barnes takes them as substantially the same in nature, arising from opposition, contempt, persecution and want, the very things the Lord met through his public life. Robertson parses the genitive as subjective, Christ's own sufferings overflowing so that we become fellow sufferers, with the corollary that partnership in suffering brings partnership in glory. Ellicott presses the union hardest: they are what Christ endured on earth, thought of as passing from him to every member of his body in his mysterious union with the Church, that they too may drink the cup he drank. Calvin arrives there by another road, distinguishing the miseries common to good and bad alike — in the wicked tokens of the curse, showing nothing but anger and participation with Adam — from the afflictions in which believers are conformed to Christ and bear his dying about in their body.

The proportion between the two is what they all seize. Gill states it plainly: as afflictions increase so do comforts. Calvin notes the clause can be read actively, so that the more he is tried the more resources he has for comforting others, but prefers the passive, that God multiplied his consolations by the measure of his tribulations — the experience David acknowledges when he says that according to the multitude of his anxieties within him God's consolations delighted his soul. Clarke turns the proportion into an argument and then an image. Because the consolation was always matched to the trial, they stood as firmly in the heaviest as in the lightest, from which he draws the encouragement that a man upheld in a slight trial need not fear a great one. Then the illustration: is it not as easy for a man to lift a hundred pounds' weight as for an infant to lift a few ounces? The proportion of strength destroys the comparative difficulty. Wesley states the same balance as an inequality — the sufferings were many and the comfort one, and yet not only equal to but overbalancing them all.

The turn by which affliction becomes the readers' benefit draws Chrysostom's warmest comment. Faint not because we are afflicted, he paraphrases, for this were rather a reason for good cheer: had we not been afflicted, this had been the ruin of you all, since had fear kept us from preaching your situation were desperate. Then, so as not to bring the encomium round to himself, Paul makes them sharers by adding that the comfort works in their patient enduring of the same sufferings — and Chrysostom asks what humility can compare with this, that men falling so far short of him are raised to the same dignity of endurance. Barnes notices the tact of it: nothing binds us more tenderly to a man than knowing he was afflicted on our account. Ellicott distinguishes the two nouns, consolation giving the inward side and salvation the outward, and insists the deliverance is seen not in escaping sufferings but in enduring them. A textual problem is on record too. Clarke reports a strange variation in the manuscripts, prints the transposed order he prefers and points to Griesbach, while Calvin reports that some of the most ancient Greek copies move the clause about hope into the middle — a reading Bloomfield preferred, judging the evidence for it exceedingly strong and for the common reading exceedingly weak. Henry and Gill keep to the upshot, that the readers' faith should not be weakened by what they see but their consolations increased.
8:
What the trouble in Asia was, nobody knows, and the corpus is unusually frank about it. Barnes lays out the candidates with their objections: the persecution at Lystra, too long past for language this fresh; the Jews lying in wait as Paul was about to go to Macedonia, which Semler preferred; and the riot of Demetrius at Ephesus, which most take, though Whitby and Macknight object that since Paul did not enter the theatre he ran no risk justifying the words about despairing of life, and refer it instead to his fighting with beasts. Clarke adds the stoning at Lystra, which did destroy his life so that his raising was miraculous, but thinks it likelier some terrible persecution recorded nowhere, of which the Corinthians had been told. Wesley and Calvin take it for the tumult in Acts, Calvin noting that Luke never intimates the extent of the danger, but that anyone knows the effect of a popular tumult once kindled. Robertson refuses to choose, saying only that we do not know whether it was sickness or peril. Gill is more interested in why Paul tells them at all: to rebut the false apostles, who had made his failure to come a charge of lightness and inconstancy.

Ellicott dissents from the whole enterprise, with the entry's most interesting argument. Had Paul meant the Demetrius tumult he would probably have localised it by naming Ephesus, as he does elsewhere; in Asia suggests a wider range of suffering, like that in the speech at Miletus. More than that, the context leads him to bodily illness, and he presses it at the next clause: the language describes the collapse of illness far more vividly than any peril of the kind proposed, since Paul could hardly have despaired of life during a riot. On the force of the words themselves there is no disagreement. Clarke calls the original exceedingly emphatic, weighed down beyond what is credible and beyond what any natural strength could support; Robertson says flatly that it was beyond Paul's power to endure if left to himself. Calvin supplies the metaphor twice, from porters given a burden more than they can stand under and, after Chrysostom, from ships so overladen they are in danger of being lost — with the distinction that a burden may be exceeding heavy and still not above a mighty man's strength, as when Samson carried off the gates of Gaza, whereas this one was both.

The word rendered sentence occupies them next, appearing nowhere else in the New Testament. Barnes takes it as a judicial verdict and wonders whether Paul had actually been condemned to the wild beasts. Robertson reports that it always means a decision rendered, in Josephus and Polybius and the papyri alike, but concedes the Vulgate's rendering suits better here. Gill rules out both a decree of heaven and a magistrate's sentence and makes it an opinion in their own breasts, so that they looked on themselves as dead men, like the Egyptians saying we be all dead men; Calvin likewise has Paul pronouncing it upon himself, lest he seem to have had it by revelation. Ellicott alone takes it medically, as a half-technical term for the opinion a physician forms on a diagnosis, perhaps picked up from Luke, so that recovery would be a veritable resurrection; and he offers a second possibility from a cognate word frequent in Hippocrates for a virulent secretion, that the sense is they had the symptoms of a fatal disease in them. On the purpose of it Calvin breaks with Chrysostom outright. Chrysostom held that Paul did not need such a remedy but set himself forth as a pattern merely in appearance; Calvin answers that he was a man of like passions, liable not only to cold and heat but to misdirected confidence and rashness, and that this was the remedy God interposed to keep them from his mind.
10:
The phrase about so great a death draws a small disagreement about grammar. Ellicott observes that death hardly admits such a qualifying adjective, and since the word is one of quality rather than quantity, would render it so terrible a death — describing the incidents of the death that seemed so near, the bodily anguish, the sense of prostration, almost the very presence of the king of terrors. Barnes reads the word as pointing to a death peculiarly frightful in manner, probably by wild beasts, and draws the lesson: Paul regarded rescue from such a death as a kind of resurrection, and every deliverance from peril or dangerous sickness should be regarded so, since God could with infinite ease have taken our breath away. Robertson supplies the picture in the verb, to draw oneself out as from a pit, and notes that Paul had counted himself as good as dead and now faces death without fear. Clarke states the reason for the wonder in a line: the circumstances were such that no human power could avail. Gill agrees it is called a death because they were not merely in danger of it but under its sentence.

The tenses that follow raise a textual question and a devotional one. Ellicott notes the middle clause is wanting in some of the better manuscripts and stands in the future in others, and suspects it was inserted to carry the deliverance through the present as well as past and future. Calvin reports the same evidence from the other side: the older copies read the future, the present having been substituted because the future recurs immediately after — whereas the apostle repeats the word precisely in order to qualify it with we have hoped. Robertson keeps the perfect, we have set our hope and still have it. Ellicott presses what that implies, that Paul was not yet altogether free, as men would judge, from the danger of a relapse, and that life was for him a perpetual series of deliverances. Calvin turns the sequence into a rule about assurance: the Lord, by accomplishing in part what he promised, bids us hope well as to what remains, confirming his promises by as many pledges as we have received favours. Clarke says it briefly: having had such signal evidence of the interposition already, they confide that it continues.

The clause about their prayers is the chapter's hardest sentence, and they say so. Barnes calls the construction very perplexing in the original, and Robertson, having parsed it, concludes that it is indeed a difficult sentence to understand. The difficulty is the word rendered persons, which Robertson counts twelve times in this epistle and takes as face in eight, preferring that pictorial sense here: out of many upturned faces thanks may be given. Ellicott weighs the same possibility and adds a point about the history of language: the noun was then beginning to move toward the sense of a character or person, in which theology would later fix it, so that if that is the meaning here it is among the earliest instances. He also insists the gift in question, mere safety and health, deserves the name as truly as prophecy or tongues. On the substance they agree. Gill ascribes the deliverance solely to God as author while allowing the prayers of the saints as helping causes; Wesley notes they help as well as other churches; Clarke observes that even an apostle felt the prayers of the Church necessary, and sets out the exchange, that the prayers of many obtain the gift and the thanksgiving of many acknowledge the mercy. Calvin finds a further advantage beyond the help, a higher manifestation of God's glory, since a favour granted to the prayers of many is acknowledged by many. Ellicott notices the delicacy of the request, which asks for prayer only by assuming they already pray and that their prayers help.
12:
Chrysostom sees why the boast comes here. Having ascribed everything to God's mercies and their prayers, Paul might make the hearer supine; so he shows they had contributed something properly their own, a conscience pure and without guile, which avails not merely to comfort but to something greater, to glorying — teaching them not to sink under afflictions but, if their conscience is pure, to be proud of them, while gently hitting at the false apostles. Henry gives the witness its standing: conscience is instead of a thousand witnesses, God's deputy in the soul, and its voice is the voice of God; what it testified concerned the constant tenour of their life, by which we judge ourselves rather than by this or that single act. Gill enters a limitation the others do not: the glorying is before men, not before God. Barnes admits the connexion is not obvious and reports that Doddridge, Locke, Macknight and Bloomfield make the good life a reason why he might expect their prayers; he prefers the wider context, that a man lately without hope of life found his confidence in having lived holily, since a good conscience lets a man always look calmly on death.

The two nouns are then taken apart, Clarke doing the etymology for everyone. Simplicity is the not-compounded, having one end in view and no sinister purpose; sincerity comes from the bright shining of the sun, and means such purity of affection as can stand God's light falling on it without the discovery of a single blemish. Robertson puts the second as the God-kind of sincerity, on the pattern of the God-kind of righteousness. Wesley says the same in his own idiom: one end in view, aiming singly at God's glory, without any tincture of guile. On the first word, Clarke and Ellicott both report that many manuscripts read holiness rather than simplicity, and Ellicott judges the better ones to do so. His best paragraph is on the verb rendered had our conversation, derived from turning back again: a continual coming back to the point from which one set out, a circulation, beginning and continuing and ending everything to the glory of God, acting toward God as the planets toward the sun, deriving all their light and heat and motion from him and incessantly revolving round him. Thus acted Paul, he adds, and the primitive Christians.

The next verse turns on a pun the corpus cannot render. Robertson and Ellicott both note the play between the verb for reading and the compound for knowing fully, and Robertson asks whether the added preposition means reading between the lines. Ellicott paraphrases: I have no hidden meaning in what I write and you read; what you read you read aright in its plain sense, and I hope the more you know me the more you will so judge me. Calvin sharpens it: the second verb means more than the first, since a man may be silently convinced a thing is true and still not own it. He complains that the ambiguity has led to misinterpretation, and dismisses Ambrose's qualification as foreign to the words. Clarke takes the reading to be the first epistle itself. On the qualifying phrase they divide: Barnes and Clarke take it to mean that some of them acknowledged him, a part conceding his uprightness while a faction denied it, whereas Ellicott makes it the measure of the justice done him. Gill allows both senses. What follows is mutual. Calvin states it best: it was pious glorying in Paul that he had brought them under obedience to Christ, and in them that they had been trained by such an apostle; by listening too readily to the spiteful they would deprive themselves of it. Barnes and Robertson add that the boast is reciprocal and reaches to the day of the Lord, Robertson noting that Titus's report showed the majority now understood him.
15:
The itinerary is reconstructed differently by different hands, and the difference matters because the charge against Paul turns on it. Ellicott gives the fullest version: the original plan was to sail straight from Ephesus to Corinth, then on to Macedonia, then back to Corinth, and thence to Jerusalem; by the time he wrote the earlier letter he had already modified it by deciding to go to Macedonia first. The point of that scheme was that the Corinthians were to have two visits and not one, which is why Ellicott can ask whether Paul had shown them less regard in the change for which he was taunted. Barnes agrees that the first purpose was to pass through Corinth on the way to Macedonia, and that in the event he went by Troas instead. Gill turns the same route into evidence of affection, since Paul might have taken, as he finally did, a nearer way to Macedonia than by Corinth. Clarke dissents. He takes the plan to have been Macedonia first and Corinth on the return, probably to winter there, and reads the phrase to mean that Paul would sail up the Aegean leaving Corinth to the west; he rejects the suggestion that Achaia was to be taken on the outward leg, since it lay considerably out of the way and could scarcely be crossed without passing close by Corinth.

What the second benefit was, and even what word stands there, is disputed. Clarke reports that several manuscripts read joy rather than grace, but judges grace the better sense; Robertson allows the other reading on the authority of Westcott and Hort, and says it would be a real second blessing if they had two visits. Calvin reports that Chrysostom takes the word in the sense of joy and says he does not much object, though he thinks the usual sense the simpler. On the content of the two benefits Clarke and Calvin differ instructively. Clarke makes the first the sowing of the seed of life by the preaching of the gospel and the second its watering. Calvin makes the first Paul's eighteen months of labour among them and the second their confirmation in the faith by a fresh visit — then turns it into an accusation, since by their own ingratitude the Corinthians had hindered his coming and deprived themselves of that second benefit, paying the penalty of their own fault and having no ground to blame Paul. Robertson supplies the grammar of the opening clause, an imperfect picturing Paul's former state of mind; Wesley glosses the phrase about confidence and adds nothing more.

Ellicott makes much of the verb in the last clause. Paul did not merely intend to go from Corinth to Judea; he expected the Corinthians to further his intentions, to escort him solemnly to the ship, perhaps to accompany him into Asia. Robertson notes the same verb serves for the office he hoped the Roman Christians would perform for his projected journey to Spain, and adds the sentence that explains the passage: the anti-Pauline party took advantage of the change of plan to criticise him sharply for vacillation and flippancy, since it is easy to find fault with the preacher, and so Paul has to explain his conduct. Barnes fills in the errand at the far end, that the object of going to Judea was to carry the collection he had been at such pains to gather among the Gentile churches. Henry draws the moral, and it is the soberest thing in the entry: good men should be careful to preserve the reputation of sincerity and constancy, should not resolve except upon mature deliberation, and should not change what they have resolved but for weighty reasons — from which the Corinthians might have concluded that the reasons here were weighty.
17:
The charge is named at last, and the word weighed. Barnes takes the noun as lightness in weight, applied to the mind in the sense of levity or fickleness, and reads the interrogative form as a sharp denial that the promise was made thoughtlessly. He is equally exact about the next phrase: to purpose according to the flesh is to form plans promoting one's own ease, such as men of the world form under earthly desires and abandon whenever they prove inconvenient. Barnes adds that probably no man ever lived who formed his plans less for the gratification of the flesh. Robertson supplies the grammar: the particle demands an indignant negative, and the noun is a late word for levity found nowhere else in the New Testament. Gill answers on the facts rather than the vocabulary, asking whether the promise was ever made absolutely, without the condition attached: had he not said he would come shortly, if the Lord will? Clarke puts the accusation as two questions: was the purpose formed without due consideration, and was it abandoned through fickleness of mind?

Ellicott raises a question none of the others asks: when had the Corinthians ever heard of the plan Paul is defending, since it was abandoned before the first epistle was sent? Either it was announced in a lost letter, or Timothy, who set out before that letter was written, was authorised to announce it; and Ellicott concedes that either is possible and no evidence decides between them. He then makes the suggestion that gives the passage its interest. The words Paul dwells on had plainly been used of him by others, and it looks as though a teacher of the circumcision party, when the first epistle arrived and showed the plan abandoned, had quoted with a sneer the rule that yes should be yes and no no — the rule of the Sermon on the Mount and of the epistle of James. If so, the passage is indirectly a reference to our Lord's teaching, and shows that the words of the Lord Jesus were habitually cited as rules of life. Robertson reaches the same two parallels by philology alone. Calvin approaches from the other end, naming the two faults that keep men's purposes from being performed, changing them almost hourly and forming them rashly, and observing that God punishes those who determine as though not subject to his will by defeating their plans and often holding them up to ridicule.

The oath that follows is read the same way by all and put to a different use by one. Barnes takes it as a solemn appeal equivalent to as the Lord liveth, and finds the argument in it: God's faithfulness is why Paul held himself bound to be faithful too. Ellicott notes the formula is one of Paul's usual assertions, though here more of the nature of an oath, and that the vague word rendered our word covers preaching, writing and personal intercourse alike. Gill supplies the insinuation being answered, that a man who had not kept his word about coming was not to be depended on in his ministry either. Calvin sees Paul doing something deliberate with it. He transfers the calumny from his person to his doctrine, unwilling that his apostleship should be defamed while not greatly concerned for his own reputation otherwise — and is honest enough to add that it does not follow that a man faithful in doctrine is observant of truth in everything else. What the oath asserts, on his reading, is that the truth of the preaching is as stable as God is faithful and true. Robertson states it in five words, that Paul is not a Yes and No man; Clarke adds that it was uncertainty about their state that made him postpone; Wesley glosses the phrase as the whole tenor of the doctrine.
19:
Barnes sets out the structure of the argument before glossing anything. Paul gives two reasons why he held himself bound to the strictest veracity: Christ always showed it, and God is always true to his promises; and since Paul served both, the obligation was sacred. On the phrase naming Christ, Barnes reports that the best commentators ancient and modern agree with Bloomfield that his doctrine is meant, so the claim is about the preaching, which never represented him as fickle. Ellicott states the same argument and then concedes its weakness with unusual candour. Forensically this was hardly an adequate defence against a charge of inconsistency; it was, he says, an argument of ethical congruity, resting on the improbability that a man who preached the absolutely true Christ, who enforced every precept with his emphatic verily, verily, should afterwards be shamelessly untruthful and palter with a double sense. He counts the word as he goes: thirty-one times in Matthew, fourteen in Mark, seven in Luke, twenty-five in its doubled form in John. Robertson makes the appeal in a sentence, that Paul cites the life of Christ to sustain his own veracity.

The two names attached to Paul's own draw separate attention. Ellicott treats the mention as an undesigned coincidence with the account in Acts of Silas coming with Timothy to join Paul at Corinth, which he takes to prove Silas and Silvanus the same man; and the three names stand in this order at the head of both Thessalonian letters. Barnes fills in the biography: Silvanus was imprisoned with Paul at Philippi, was with him when he first came to Corinth, and was trusted enough to have his name joined to Paul's in several epistles. Calvin asks why Apollos goes unmentioned while these two are named, and answers that the more a man was assailed by calumniators the more careful Paul was to defend him. He then presses what the naming is for. The preaching contained nothing but Christ alone, the eternal and immutable truth of God; and since Christ is often disfigured by the inventions of men, Paul claims to have held him forth pure and undisguised, not varying his doctrine so as to present him in a new shape after the manner of Proteus. Clarke turns it back to the argument: had he been a worldly man, he must have had the same secular interest in view when he first preached to them.

On the promises there is a textual point and one small disagreement. Ellicott reports that many of the better manuscripts read instead, in him is the Yea, wherefore also by him is the Amen to God for glory by our means, and judges the thought unchanged either way: the promises are fulfilled and ratified in Christ, who was as it were a living incarnate Amen to them. He and Barnes both connect this with Amen as a name of Christ, the faithful and true witness; Robertson connects it instead with the Amen of public worship. Clarke distributes the two words between the ends of the transaction, the promise coming originally by Christ and so yea, having its fulfilment through him and so amen; Wesley distributes them four ways — yea with respect to God promising and amen with respect to men believing, yea with respect to the apostles and amen with respect to their hearers. Calvin fixes the principle underneath: all the promises rest on Christ alone, which depends in turn on there being no other in whom the Father is propitious to us; and it were worse than absurd to think that one in whom they are all established should himself be wavering and unsteady. The one division is over the closing words: Barnes takes the glory to be produced through Christians generally, Ellicott insists the context fixes it on the preacher, and Gill and Clarke leave it with the ministry.
21:
The defence turns into doxology, and everyone notices the pronoun. Barnes observes that Paul, having dwelt at length on his own fidelity, now traces it all to God to prevent any appearance of boasting; the first us is himself, the second takes in the Corinthians. Ellicott sees the same anxiety in the added words with you, characteristic of a man unwilling to claim for himself what others might not claim with equal right. Robertson supplies a local touch on the first verb: an apt metaphor in Corinth, where confirming a bargain was a familiar transaction. Ellicott would render the next phrase into Christ rather than in him, as though the establishing resulted in actual incorporation, which he thinks truer than paraphrasing it as confirmation in believing; and he dates the anointing to a definite moment, baptism or the laying on of hands, when the first-fruits of the Spirit were received. Barnes adds that kings, prophets and priests were anointed on entering office, the rite being emblematic of the Spirit's influences. Calvin turns it inward: God always has his Amen, but such is our vanity that we do not utter ours in return except when he testifies surely in our hearts by his Spirit, since to keep pace with God in steadfastness is not in man's power.

On the seal they divide by profession rather than by school. Robertson goes to the papyri, where the verb has a wide legal use, giving validity to documents and guaranteeing goods by sealing sacks and chests. Gill catalogues the uses of seals — property, distinction, affection, protection, concealment — then chooses the certifying sense, the assurance God gives his people of their interest in his love. Ellicott makes it the seal of a covenant attesting its validity, citing the Jewish practice of sealing deeds. Barnes takes the same line and insists on what it is not: nothing miraculous, nothing of the nature of direct revelation, but the ordinary operations of the Spirit producing repentance, faith, hope and joy, which are themselves the evidence. Clarke alone reads it of the ministry rather than of believers generally, taking the miraculous gifts to have attested their extraordinary calling and to preserve them from dissimulation and falsity of every kind. Wesley has God stamping his image on the heart and so marking us as his own property. Cyril puts the verse to a use none of the others attempt, citing it among the proofs that Paul and his fellow apostles were full of the Holy Ghost.

The last word draws the chapter's best philology. Ellicott traces it from a Hebrew verb meaning to mix or to pledge, transliterated into the Greek of Genesis, carried by Phoenician traders to Greece, Carthage and Rome, used by an Attic orator and by Plautus and Terence, then shortened in Roman law because the full form was felt vulgar, and surviving into Italian, modern French and even popular Scotch. As Paul uses it, he says, it was a condensed parable that people in commercial cities would readily understand: their past spiritual experience had no character of finality, being rather the pledge of greater gifts to come. Clarke reaches the same source independently, identifying the word with the pledge Judah gave Tamar, and draws a hard conclusion: he who is found with the earnest of God's Spirit in his heart shall have the life of which it is the pledge, and without it there can be no glory. Wesley marks the distinction the English blurs: a pledge is restored when the debt is paid, but an earnest is not taken away, only completed. Robertson uses the modern phrase, earnest money, part payment on the whole obligation, then turns it back into the argument: God has done all this, and God is Paul's pledge that he is sincere and will come to Corinth in due time.
23:
The real reason arrives at last, under oath. Barnes reports Rosenmuller's judgment that the second chapter ought to have begun here, the transition being sharper than at the actual division, as Tindal's division had it. He then sets out Paley's reconstruction, established, he thinks, with something near moral certainty: the change of purpose was made before the first epistle, Paul having decided to try the effect of a letter and let the church discipline the chief offender itself; he said nothing then of the change, and only now, the letter having had its effect, gives the true reason. Ellicott corrects the rendering twice, making it a calling of God to witness against his own soul, and insisting the adverb cannot mean not yet: the sense is that he came no more, not a second time. Robertson quotes Plummer that calling heaven to witness is frequent from Homer onwards; Gill treats the words as a full oath, as if Paul had said, I swear by the living God, the searcher of hearts. Wesley draws his own inference: was Paul not speaking by the Spirit, and can a more solemn oath be conceived? Who then can imagine that Christ designed to forbid all swearing?

Chrysostom alone sees a contradiction and will not smooth it over. What sayest thou, O blessed Paul? To spare them thou camest not? A little above thou saidst thou camest not because thou purposest not according to the flesh, nor art thine own master, but art led by the authority of the Spirit; here thou sayest it was thine own act. He offers three ways out. Either this too was of the Spirit, who urged the motive of sparing them; or he speaks of some other coming, meaning that before the first letter he had meant to come and restrained himself for love's sake lest he find them unamended; or, after the second letter, the Spirit no longer forbidding, he stayed away of his own accord. Chrysostom prefers the last, with the Spirit forbidding at first and Paul concurring afterwards on his own conviction. Calvin reads the verse as an indirect reproach: it would be unfair that Paul be grieved through their fault, and worse that they assent to a calumny putting an innocent man in the place of the guilty. Clarke assembles the state of Paul's reputation from the letters: his doctrine opposed, his apostleship questioned, himself despised as a man who dared not come. Wesley notices a nicety: Paul says elegantly to Corinth, and not to you, at the moment he intimates his power to punish.

The retraction in the last verse is felt by all to be deliberate. Ellicott puts it best: Paul has scarcely uttered words implying authority when the thought comes that he may seem to claim too much, so he shrinks from lording it over God's heritage and half apologises for so strong a word as sparing, knowing they have a standing-ground in their faith independently of him. Robertson gives the figure its rhetorical name, a delicate correction of a misapprehension. Gill says the words are added lest anyone think the ministers assumed tyrannical power over the churches, and Calvin frames it as an objection anticipated: do you then act so tyrannically? Barnes and Clarke draw the same distinction, Clarke pushing it furthest. The apostles did have the right to prescribe articles of belief, a dominion over faith essential to their office; but they refused to exercise it in a lordly manner, appealing to reason and employing persuasion, light and love. Then Clarke turns on those who claimed the right without the warrant, men neither apostles nor infallible, insisting on new doctrines taught nowhere by apostles and threatening perdition to those who would not credit them. Did they succeed? Yes, for a time; and that time was a time of thick darkness, a darkness that might be felt, producing nothing but misery.
